# Two jars {#sec-two-jars .unnumbered} *Roughly 15 minutes. Nothing here gets resolved. That is deliberate, and it is next week.* ## Part A: the question you actually have Nobody writes a grant to find the mean mass of a bean. Real questions are comparative: treated against control, site against site, before against after. You do not want to know what the mean **is**. You want to know whether **these differ from those**. So: a second jar. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} sample_control <- population |> slice_sample(n = 10) |> mutate(jar = "Control") sample_treated <- population_treated |> slice_sample(n = 10) |> mutate(jar = "Treated") two_samples <- bind_rows(sample_control, sample_treated) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display}
|jar | n| mean_g| sd_g| se_g| lower| upper| |:-------|--:|------:|---------:|---------:|---------:|---------:| |Control | 10| 0.5483| 0.0665517| 0.0210455| 0.5006918| 0.5959082| |Treated | 10| 0.5464| 0.0881995| 0.0278911| 0.4833059| 0.6094941|
::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(two_samples, aes(x = jar, y = mass_g, colour = jar, shape = jar)) + geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0), alpha = 0.4, size = 2) + geom_pointrange(data = summary_table, aes(x = jar, y = mean_g, ymin = lower, ymax = upper), linewidth = 0.7, size = 0.8) + colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 3") + labs(x = NULL, y = "Bean mass (g), mean with 95% CI") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "none") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Ten beans from each jar. Small points are individual beans; the interval is the 95% confidence interval on each mean.](05-two-jars_files/figure-html/fig-two-jars-1.png){#fig-two-jars fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Part B: Box 3 The intervals overlap. Look at your prediction sheet; most of the room wrote that this means no difference. **Overlapping 95% confidence intervals mean there is no significant difference between the groups.** :::{.callout-important} ## It is wrong Not imprecise. Wrong, and wrong in a direction nobody expects. Cumming [@cumming2009] worked out what overlap corresponds to. For two independent 95% intervals, when they **just touch** the p-value is about **0.01**, not 0.05, and they can **overlap by roughly half the length of one arm** before p reaches 0.05. The eyeball rule is not merely rough, it is **conservative**: you will declare no difference when there is one, repeatedly, and nothing will tell you. That is before the other half of the problem, whether the bars are SDs, SEs or CIs at all. Belia and colleagues [@belia2005] found 473 authors could not reliably tell CI bars from SE bars. **Always state in the axis label what your error bars are.** This book does, every time. Now you know why. ::: ## Part C: what is missing You cannot answer the two-jar question with what you have, because the object you need does not exist yet. The **difference between two means** is itself an estimate: it came from data, it would differ with different beans, so it has its own sampling distribution and its own standard error. A third wall, not of beans, not of means, but of differences between means. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} draw_difference <- function(n = 10) { mean(sample(population_treated$mass_g, n)) - mean(sample(population$mass_g, n)) } many_differences <- tibble(replicate = 1:10000) |> mutate(difference = map_dbl(replicate, \(i) draw_difference(n = 10))) many_differences |> summarise(mean_difference = mean(difference), se_difference = sd(difference)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| mean_difference| se_difference| |---------------:|-------------:| | 0.0259264| 0.0367382|
::: ::: **Before you run the next chunk: the SE of the difference, compared with the two individual SEs, is:** :::{.callout-warning} ## The trap ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble( quantity = c("SE of the difference (simulated)", "Difference of the two SEs", "Sum of the two SEs"), value = c(sd(many_differences$difference), abs(summary_table$se_g[2] - summary_table$se_g[1]), sum(summary_table$se_g)) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|quantity | value| |:--------------------------------|---------:| |SE of the difference (simulated) | 0.0367382| |Difference of the two SEs | 0.0068457| |Sum of the two SEs | 0.0489366|
::: ::: None of the arithmetic you would guess is right. Uncertainties do not combine the way quantities combine. Two uncertain things compared give you something *more* uncertain than either, but not as much more as adding would suggest. How they actually combine is the first thing next week. ::: ## Part D: next week With the difference-wall in hand, one question becomes askable: > Suppose the two jars are identical. How often would a difference as big as mine turn up anyway? That is a **p-value**. It is not the probability the jars are the same, nor the probability your result is a fluke. It is the third costume of the inversion from the last chapter, and you should see it coming. Then: the difference of two means and how its SE really works; the p-value, defined once, built by shuffling labels rather than by formula; **Type I and Type II errors**, which need a decision rule to be errors about; and Box 3, resolved. Bring the sheet. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Three things before next week (graded) :::: ::::{.task-container} 1. Rerun with **n = 100** per jar. Do the intervals still overlap? Has anything about the jars changed? 2. Set `population_treated` to `mean = 0.52`, identical to control. Run twenty times with different seeds. How often do the intervals fail to overlap even though the jars are truly identical? What have you measured? 3. Predict, in writing, before next week: if the SE of a difference is neither the difference nor the sum of the SEs, what is it? You have the pieces. Wrong answers count. :::: :::
You have measured something with a name that you meet formally next week. With both jars identical there is no difference at all, so any separation is manufactured entirely by which beans you drew. Do it twenty times and the intervals will fail to overlap occasionally; had you stopped on that run and written it up, you would have reported a difference that does not exist. Notice how few runs it takes, and that nothing in the output warns you, because there is no such thing as a figure that looks like a false positive. Do not put a number on the rate yet. You find that number next week, and it has a Greek letter.
:::{.callout-note} ## The recurring question Each point in @fig-two-jars is a bean weighed once. Suppose instead you had 10 beans and weighed each ten times, then plotted all 100 measurements with a confidence interval. The figure would look tighter. Would it be better? :::
